pull.title: silentpayments: reject label tweaks that overflow the group order
pull.body: Label tweaks returned by the `label_lookup` callback that overflow the group order were silently reduced. `recipient_label_create` never produces such tweaks, so an overflowing one means the caller's label cache is broken. As suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/1929#issuecomment-6310143782, this PR treats it as API misuse using `ARG_CHECK` (illegal callback, return 0), documents the requirement. It also adds a test and a changelog entry.

Concept ACK

I tend to thinkl the Changelog entry really adds more confusion then it solves. Any caller who hits this is clearly violates the API contract (in a very weird way).

tACK b5fb2adf090d49b034db86b60a740d6058743ff7

I built the head with CMake on macOS arm64 and ran ctest: all 231 tests pass. I also wrote a small program against the public API that scans a one-output labeled transaction with several tweaks in the label cache, and ran it against the head and the merge base. With the tweak from `recipient_label_create`, both find the output and return a tweak that spends it. With the group order or 2^256-1, the merge base returns 1 and a tweak that does not spend the output. The head calls the illegal callback, returns 0, reports no found outputs and leaves the found-output entry untouched. I can share the program if useful.

Under valgrind's constant-time check, the new `if (tweak_overflow)` branches on a secret value when the label tweak is marked secret.

I added to `ctime_tests` a scan that finds an output sent to a labeled address, with the scan key and the label tweak (the value `label_lookup` returns) marked secret, and ran it under valgrind. Valgrind reports "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)" at `if (tweak_overflow) {` in `secp256k1_silentpayments_recipient_scan_outputs`. The same test gives 0 errors on the base commit. With the one-line `secp256k1_declassify` suggested inline, the run is clean and the output is still found.

I can post the test here, or open a follow-up PR that adds it to `src/ctime_tests.c`.

events.message:
silentpayments: reject label tweaks that overflow the group order

Previously, a label tweak returned by the `label_lookup` callback that
is not smaller than the group order was silently reduced modulo the
group order. Such a tweak can never be produced by
`secp256k1_silentpayments_recipient_label_create`, so it indicates a
corrupted or improperly constructed label cache, i.e., a bug on the
caller side rather than invalid data from an untrusted source. Treat
this as an API misuse (similar to the magic byte checks on the
`prevouts_summary` argument), and add a test.

The assignment of the found output is moved after the label tweak
check, so that the found_outputs[k] entry is left untouched if the
scan is aborted due to an invalid label tweak.

events.body:
tACK 95552e1654bfd3d34facfcf64e7ca3b0a52594c0

Since my test of b5fb2adf, `git range-diff` shows only the header doc changes dropped, from the commit and its message; the code and the test are unchanged. On Linux aarch64 (gcc 14.2, valgrind 3.24, no asm), `make check` passes and `ctime_tests` gives 0 errors under valgrind, on the head and on the head merged with master a3a5cd4 ([patch, commands and logs](https://gist.github.com/fametrano/a9d03e33232e80126603c5f2f2f4f424/434ba3302b4880408bdbc359d7ffecad88dd77f8)).

The [inline thread](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/1974#discussion_r4441199716) mentions a ctime failure left in the tree. The only one I know of is the one I reported in that thread, from a scan I added, and that scan is not in the tree. `ctime_tests` gives 0 errors with or without the `secp256k1_declassify` line, because its scan passes no label lookup, which its comment says is sufficient, and never reaches `if (tweak_overflow)`. With my scan, which finds a labeled output, valgrind reports 0 errors with only the scan key marked secret. With the label tweak marked secret too, it reports 1 error at `if (tweak_overflow)`. The declassify line removes that error, and the merge base gives 0 errors on the same test. So this only matters if the label tweak counts as secret, and even then the branch reveals only that a caller passed an invalid tweak, which `recipient_label_create` never returns. It does not block the PR.

That question, including Yudis-bit's point about clearing the tweak, stays open for the follow-up theStack proposed. If the answer is that the tweak is secret, the fix is [my one-line suggestion](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/1974#discussion_r4356645923), and my scan can go into `ctime_tests` with it.

comments.body: Would prefer to do this in a follow-up PR, where we can discuss whether the label-related values need to be treated as secret in the context of the scanning function in the first place (I'd lean towards no, but curious about other opinions).

Do we need the docs changes at all? If I understand correctly, the way the API is designed is that label tweaks are opaque to the caller, and they should use `secp256k1_silentpayments_recipient_label_create` to create one. Talking about scalars will only confuse the user.

Good point, dropped the docs changes, adapted the commit message and PR description accordingly. Mentioning low-level details like scalars and group order for user types in the API docs seems counter-productive indeed.

Hm, but the comment right below line 760 explicitly says:
> /* Leaking these values would break indistinguishability of the transaction, so clear them. */

and clears `label_tweak_scalar`. If leaking it breaks indistinguishability, treating it as public seems inconsistent with the cleanup in this very PR.

Also `secp256k1_declassify` is a no-op outside valgrind/msan builds anyway, so adding it here avoids leaving a known ctime test failure in the tree.
